codes.name: Continue
codes.description: The server has received the request headers and the client should proceed to send the request body.
codes.usage: Used with the Expect header when a client wants to send a large body. The server responds with 100 Continue to indicate the client should proceed.

codes.name: Switching Protocols
codes.description: The requester has asked the server to switch protocols and the server has agreed to do so.
codes.usage: Commonly used for WebSocket upgrades. The client sends an Upgrade header and the server responds with 101 to confirm the protocol switch.

codes.name: Processing
codes.description: The server has received and is processing the request, but no response is available yet.
codes.usage: Used in WebDAV to prevent the client from timing out while the server processes a long request.

codes.name: Early Hints
codes.description: Used to return some response headers before final HTTP message.
codes.usage: Allows a server to send preliminary headers (like Link headers for preloading resources) before the final response is ready.

codes.name: OK
codes.description: The request has succeeded. The meaning varies depending on the HTTP method used.
codes.usage: Standard response for successful HTTP requests. GET returns the resource, POST returns the result of the action, etc.

codes.name: Created
codes.description: The request has been fulfilled and resulted in a new resource being created.
codes.usage: Typically sent after a POST request that creates a new resource. The Location header should contain the URL of the new resource.

codes.name: Accepted
codes.description: The request has been accepted for processing, but the processing has not been completed.
codes.usage: Used for asynchronous operations where the server has accepted the request but hasn't completed it yet (e.g., batch processing).

codes.name: Non-Authoritative Information
codes.description: The server is a transforming proxy that received a 200 OK but is returning a modified version of the response.
codes.usage: Used by proxies when they modify the response before forwarding it to the client.

codes.name: No Content
codes.description: The server successfully processed the request and is not returning any content.
codes.usage: Commonly used for DELETE requests or when updating a resource without returning the updated version.

codes.name: Reset Content
codes.description: The server successfully processed the request, but is not returning any content. Requires the requester to reset the document view.
codes.usage: Used to reset a form or UI state after a successful submission.

codes.name: Partial Content
codes.description: The server is delivering only part of the resource due to a range header sent by the client.
codes.usage: Used for resuming downloads or streaming media. The client sends a Range header and the server responds with 206 and the requested portion.

codes.name: Multi-Status
codes.description: The message body contains multiple status codes for multiple independent operations.
codes.usage: Used in WebDAV when a single request affects multiple resources, each with its own status.

codes.name: Already Reported
codes.description: Used inside a DAV:propstat response element to avoid enumerating members of multiple bindings to the same collection repeatedly.
codes.usage: WebDAV-specific status to avoid duplicate entries in responses.

codes.name: IM Used
codes.description: The server has fulfilled a GET request for the resource, and the response is a representation of the result of instance-manipulations applied to the current instance.
codes.usage: Used with delta encoding to indicate that the response is a delta applied to the current instance.

codes.name: Multiple Choices
codes.description: Indicates multiple options for the resource from which the client may choose.
codes.usage: Used when a resource has multiple representations (e.g., different formats, languages). The response should include a list of options.

codes.name: Moved Permanently
codes.description: This and all future requests should be directed to the given URI.
codes.usage: Used for permanent URL redirects. Search engines transfer SEO value to the new URL. The Location header contains the new URL.

codes.name: Found
codes.description: The resource resides temporarily under a different URI. The client should continue to use the original URI.
codes.usage: Used for temporary redirects. Often misused for permanent redirects (should use 301 instead).

codes.name: See Other
codes.description: The response to the request can be found under another URI using a GET method.
codes.usage: Used after a POST request to redirect to a result page. Prevents resubmission of the form if the user refreshes.

codes.name: Not Modified
codes.description: Indicates that the resource has not been modified since the version specified by the request headers.
codes.usage: Used for conditional requests with If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match headers. Enables efficient caching.

codes.name: Use Proxy
codes.description: The requested resource is available only through a proxy, the address for which is provided in the response.
codes.usage: Deprecated. Most clients do not implement this status code due to security concerns.

codes.name: Temporary Redirect
codes.description: The resource resides temporarily under a different URI. The method and body must not be changed.
codes.usage: Like 302 but guarantees the method and body will not be changed on redirect. Used when the redirect must preserve the HTTP method.

codes.name: Permanent Redirect
codes.description: The resource has been permanently moved to a new URL. The method and body must not be changed.
codes.usage: Like 301 but guarantees the method and body will not be changed on redirect. The modern replacement for 301 when method preservation is needed.

codes.name: Bad Request
codes.description: The server cannot or will not process the request due to an apparent client error.
codes.usage: Generic error for malformed requests, invalid syntax, or missing required parameters.

codes.name: Unauthorized
codes.description: Authentication is required and has failed or has not been provided.
codes.usage: Sent when the client must authenticate itself. The WWW-Authenticate header indicates the authentication method.

codes.name: Payment Required
codes.description: Reserved for future use. Originally intended for digital payment schemes.
codes.usage: Rarely used. Some APIs use it to indicate that a payment is required to access the resource.

codes.name: Forbidden
codes.description: The client does not have permission to access the requested resource, even though it is authenticated.
codes.usage: Sent when the client is authenticated but lacks the necessary permissions. Unlike 401, re-authenticating will not help.

codes.name: Not Found
codes.description: The requested resource could not be found but may be available in the future.
codes.usage: The most common error code. Sent when the server cannot find the requested resource.

codes.name: Method Not Allowed
codes.description: A request method is not supported for the requested resource.
codes.usage: Sent when the client uses an HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.) that is not allowed for the resource. The Allow header lists allowed methods.

codes.name: Not Acceptable
codes.description: The requested resource is capable of generating only content not acceptable according to the Accept headers sent in the request.
codes.usage: Sent when the server cannot produce a response matching the client's Accept header (e.g., requested JSON but server only provides XML).

codes.name: Proxy Authentication Required
codes.description: The client must first authenticate itself with the proxy.
codes.usage: Similar to 401 but for proxy authentication. The Proxy-Authenticate header indicates the authentication method.

codes.name: Request Timeout
codes.description: The server timed out waiting for the request.
codes.usage: Sent when the client takes too long to send the complete request.

codes.name: Conflict
codes.description: The request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the resource.
codes.usage: Used for optimistic locking, duplicate entries, or when the request conflicts with the resource state.

codes.name: Gone
codes.description: The requested resource is no longer available and will not be available again.
codes.usage: Used when a resource has been intentionally removed and should not be requested again. Search engines will remove it from their index.

codes.name: Length Required
codes.description: The request did not specify the length of its content, which is required by the requested resource.
codes.usage: Sent when the server requires a Content-Length header but the client did not provide one.

codes.name: Precondition Failed
codes.description: The server does not meet one of the preconditions that the requester put on the request.
codes.usage: Used with conditional headers like If-Match or If-Unmodified-Since for optimistic concurrency control.

codes.name: Payload Too Large
codes.description: The request is larger than the server is willing or able to process.
codes.usage: Sent when the request body exceeds the server's maximum allowed size.

codes.name: URI Too Long
codes.description: The URI provided was too long for the server to process.
codes.usage: Sent when the URL exceeds the server's maximum length (typically due to too many query parameters).

codes.name: Unsupported Media Type
codes.description: The request entity has a media type which the server or resource does not support.
codes.usage: Sent when the client sends data in a format the server doesn't understand (e.g., XML when JSON is expected).

codes.name: Range Not Satisfiable
codes.description: The client has asked for a portion of the file the server cannot supply.
codes.usage: Sent when the Range header requests a byte range that doesn't exist in the resource.

codes.name: Expectation Failed
codes.description: The server cannot meet the requirements of the Expect request header field.
codes.usage: Sent when the Expect header contains an expectation the server cannot fulfill (e.g., Expect: 100-continue but server doesn't support it).

codes.name: I'm a teapot
codes.description: The server refuses to brew coffee because it is, permanently, a teapot.
codes.usage: An April Fools' joke from RFC 2324 (Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol). Sometimes used humorously or to indicate a feature is not implemented.

codes.name: Misdirected Request
codes.description: The request was directed at a server that is not able to produce a response.
codes.usage: Used in HTTP/2 when a request is sent to a server that is not authoritative for the target URI.

codes.name: Unprocessable Entity
codes.description: The request was well-formed but was unable to be followed due to semantic errors.
codes.usage: Commonly used in REST APIs when the request body is syntactically correct but contains invalid data (e.g., validation errors).

codes.name: Locked
codes.description: The resource that is being accessed is locked.
codes.usage: Used in WebDAV when a resource is locked by another client.

codes.name: Failed Dependency
codes.description: The request failed because it depended on another request and that request failed.
codes.usage: Used in WebDAV when a request in a batch depends on another request that failed.

codes.name: Too Early
codes.description: Indicates that the server is unwilling to risk processing a request that might be replayed.
codes.usage: Used with TLS 1.3 Early Data to prevent replay attacks.

codes.name: Upgrade Required
codes.description: The client should switch to a different protocol.
codes.usage: Sent when the server requires the client to upgrade to a newer protocol (e.g., from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2). The Upgrade header indicates the required protocol.

codes.name: Precondition Required
codes.description: The origin server requires the request to be conditional.
codes.usage: Used to prevent the 'lost update' problem where a client fetches a resource, modifies it, and overwrites another client's changes.

codes.name: Too Many Requests
codes.description: The user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time.
codes.usage: Used for rate limiting. The Retry-After header indicates when the client can retry.

codes.name: Request Header Fields Too Large
codes.description: The server is unwilling to process the request because either an individual header field or all the header fields collectively are too large.
codes.usage: Sent when the request headers exceed the server's maximum size (e.g., too many cookies).

codes.name: Unavailable For Legal Reasons
codes.description: The resource is unavailable due to legal demands (e.g., censorship, court orders).
codes.usage: Used when a resource is blocked for legal reasons. The name references Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451.

codes.name: Internal Server Error
codes.description: A generic error message, given when an unexpected condition was encountered and no more specific message is suitable.
codes.usage: The catch-all error for server-side issues. Should be logged and investigated.

codes.name: Not Implemented
codes.description: The server either does not recognize the request method, or it lacks the ability to fulfil the request.
codes.usage: Sent when the server doesn't support the requested functionality (e.g., a new HTTP method).

codes.name: Bad Gateway
codes.description: The server was acting as a gateway or proxy and received an invalid response from the upstream server.
codes.usage: Common in reverse proxy setups (Nginx, HAProxy) when the backend server returns an invalid response.

codes.name: Service Unavailable
codes.description: The server is currently unavailable (overloaded or down for maintenance).
codes.usage: Used during maintenance windows or when the server is overloaded. The Retry-After header can indicate when to retry.

codes.name: Gateway Timeout
codes.description: The server was acting as a gateway or proxy and did not receive a timely response from the upstream server.
codes.usage: Sent when a proxy server times out waiting for a response from the backend.

codes.name: HTTP Version Not Supported
codes.description: The server does not support the HTTP protocol version used in the request.
codes.usage: Sent when the client uses an HTTP version the server doesn't support.

codes.name: Variant Also Negotiates
codes.description: Transparent content negotiation results in a circular reference.
codes.usage: Rare. Indicates a configuration error in content negotiation.

codes.name: Insufficient Storage
codes.description: The server is unable to store the representation needed to complete the request.
codes.usage: Used in WebDAV when the server doesn't have enough storage to complete the request.

codes.name: Loop Detected
codes.description: The server detected an infinite loop while processing the request.
codes.usage: Used in WebDAV when a recursive operation creates a loop.

codes.name: Not Extended
codes.description: Further extensions to the request are required for the server to fulfil it.
codes.usage: Rare. Indicates the client must extend the request to fulfill the server's requirements.

codes.name: Network Authentication Required
codes.description: The client needs to authenticate to gain network access.
codes.usage: Used by captive portals (e.g., WiFi hotspots) to indicate the client must authenticate before accessing the internet.
